underlying the superior performance of subtype 2 EVs. Moreover, there is no consideration
of the optimal diagnostic time window for the proposed approach.
Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their insightful comment regarding the
biological rationale for the superior performance of subtype 2 EVs. The enhanced
diagnostic capability of this subset stems from its optimal size, which uniquely balances
efficient translocation across BBB with substantial biomarker-carrying capacity. Specifically,
EVs within the 90–180 nm range are sufficiently small to traverse the BBB effectively1-3,
facilitating their release into circulation after stroke, while also providing greater membrane
surface area for robust presentation of cell-type-specific markers compared to smaller EVs
(<90 nm)4. Moreover, EVs larger than 180 nm often represent apoptotic bodies and exhibit
greater heterogeneity. In support of this, our proteomic analysis revealed that subtype 2
contains a significantly higher number of proteins of subcellular origin compared to both
subtype 1 (<90 nm) and subtype 3 (>180 nm) (new Supplementary Figure 12).
Regarding the optimal diagnostic time window, we agree on its critical importance for
clinical translation. In alignment with stroke management guidelines that emphasize
intervention as early as possible to prevent irreversible brain injury, we propose that blood
sampling for the SHEAF platform should be performed immediately upon patient
presentation. Notably, unlike conventional diagnostic approaches that can only be
conducted after hospital arrival, our method holds potential for prehospital use—such as
during ambulance transport—enabling significantly earlier diagnosis. This shift forward in
the diagnostic timeline allows crucial treatment decisions (e.g., thrombolysis or surgery) to
be made sooner upon arrival, thereby preserving the “time is brain” principle and improving
patient outcomes. We have revised the Discussion to highlight this advantage of early,
time-sensitive application of our approach.

Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for highlighting these important limitations
regarding our initial cohort. In direct response to the comments, we have expanded the
clinical cohort to include additional samples—specifically, 10 ICH, 10 IS, and 20 healthy
donors as a control group—which has strengthened the statistical reliability of our findings.
To improve transparency and allow for a better assessment of potential confounders, we
have also included a new patient information table (new Supplementary Table 2)
summarizing age, sex, and comorbidities. We clarify that for all stroke patients, blood was
collected prior to any treatment intervention, and the diagnosis of either ICH or IS was
confirmed within one hour after blood sampling.
While the expanded sample size represents a meaningful improvement, we acknowledge
that further scaling through larger, multicenter studies will be important to support the
broader applicability of our findings. As such, we have explicitly discussed the current
cohort size in the Discussion section, framing it as a focused foundation for future
validation. We also emphasize that this work provides a robust methodological platform
and preliminary clinical evidence, paving the way for subsequent multi-institutional
collaborations aimed at prehospital translation.

## Paper

## Abstract

Diagnosing intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) in prehospital settings remains challenging due to unavailability of immediate neuroimaging, clinical overlap with ischemic stroke, and absence of validated circulating biomarkers for time-critical settings. Extracellular vesicles (EVs), subcellular structures capable of transporting biomolecular payloads (e.g., proteins, nucleic acids) across the blood-brain barrier, have emerged as compelling diagnostic candidates for ICH. Nevertheless, their clinical translation has been impeded by inherent biophysical heterogeneity, particularly polydisperse size distributions. To address this limitation, we engineer a steric hindrance-mediated EV analysis and size fractionation (SHEAF) platform, integrating steric hindrance-based size fractionation with membrane protein profiling to stratify EVs into three size subtypes within a 45-min workflow. Systematic evaluation using the SHEAF platform reveals that the 90 - 180 nm EV subtype exhibits superior discriminative capacity in differentiating ICH from ischemic stroke plasma specimens. This technology not only advances rapid prehospital ICH diagnostics but also establishes a method for elucidating size-dependent EV functionalities across neurological pathologies.

---

## Introduction

Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and ischemic stroke (IS), the two primary stroke subtypes, differ fundamentally in pathophysiology and clinical management. ICH involves acute bleeding into the brain parenchyma, often leading to neurological deterioration due to mass effect and elevated intracranial pressure; management focuses on hemorrhage control, intensive neurocritical care, and potential surgical evacuation1,2. In contrast, IS results from cerebral artery occlusion, causing rapid neuronal death from ischemia, with treatment centered on timely reperfusion via intravenous thrombolysis or mechanical thrombectomy3,4. Critically, these therapeutic approaches are mutually exclusive: thrombolytic agents, essential in IS, are strictly contraindicated in ICH due to the risk of exacerbating hemorrhage. Moreover, each minute of untreated ischemia leads to the loss of approximately 1.9 million neurons5, while delays in ICH intervention worsen mass effect and outcomes6. Therefore, rapid and accurate differentiation between ICH and IS from symptom onset is crucial. Although neuroimaging modalities such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) serve as the diagnostic gold standard7-9, their limited availability to hospital settings hinders prehospital diagnosis and delays subtype identification. This diagnostic gap underscores the urgent need for biomarker-based diagnostic strategies. However, many candidate biomarkers, such as glial fibrillary acidic protein10,11, may lack sufficient specificity and accuracy alone, highlighting the necessity of identifying more reliable molecular markers or panels to improve diagnostic precision.

Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are bi-layered nanoparticles that encapsulate diverse molecular cargo—including nucleic acids, proteins, and saccharides. The surrounding lipid bilayer shields this cargo from degradation, which better preserves biomarker integrity compared to free-floating molecules12. This protective feature makes EVs highly sensitive and reliable circulating biomarkers for various diseases, particularly in early stages13-16. Furthermore, EVs can cross the blood-brain barrier via transcytosis, enabling non-invasive detection of brain-derived pathological signals in peripheral blood17,18. This capability is especially relevant in conditions like ICH, where elevated levels of EV biomarkers have been consistently observed19,20. However, a significant challenge in EV-based diagnostics is their high heterogeneity in native biofluids, evident in size, origin, and cargo composition. While this heterogeneity complicates analysis, it also unveils a layer of biological specificity: different EV subpopulations are now understood to carry distinct biomarker profiles and functions. For instance, emerging evidence confirms that specific size-defined EV subtypes are selectively enriched with disease-specific molecular signatures, thereby enhancing diagnostic accuracy for cancer, neurodegenerative, and cardiovascular disease21-25. Nevertheless, existing technologies for EV size subtyping remain constrained by high costs, low throughput, and risks of damaging EV integrity during isolation26-29. Addressing these limitations is essential to unlocking the full clinical diagnostic potential of EVs.

Steric hindrance at nano-interfaces reduces the activity of ligands immobilized on nanoparticle surfaces. This effect intensifies as nanoparticle size increases. For example, reduced binding efficiencies were observed for duramycin, cinnamycin, α-synuclein, and β-amyloid when interacting with phospholipids on larger EV membranes30-32. Moreover, ligand activity on nanoparticle surfaces can be modulated by tuning the grafting density and the length of inert protective chains33. Building upon these insights, we developed a steric hindrance-mediated EV analysis and size fractionation (SHEAF) platform, which integrated size-selective separation with EV membrane protein profiling into a microfluidic system. This platform revealed that the distinct protein signatures in 90 - 180 nm EVs can effectively differentiate ICH and IS plasma samples. Our work established a rapid, accurate, and user-friendly system for EV size fractionation and molecular characterization, underscoring the diagnostic significance of specific EV size subtypes in ICH assessment.

---

## Results

Design of SHEAF platform
To accomplish size-selective EV isolation through precisely controlled surface interactions, aptamers specifically targeting the EV transmembrane protein CD63 (APT ) were chemically co-immobilized with polyethylene glycol (PEG) polymer chains on magnetic nanoparticle (MNP) surface. Within this dual-functional interface, the APT ligands served as molecular recognition ligands for CD63-mediated EV binding, while the PEG created an adjustable steric barrier through their flexible polymer chains to spatially regulate ligand accessibility (Fig. 1a). Through iterative experimental optimization of two critical surface parameters - the APT grafting ratio and the PEG molecular weight (ranging from 2 kDa to 30 kDa) - three distinct MNP formulations were developed for capturing EVs with diameters below 90 nm diameter, below 180 nm, and exceeding 180 nm.

A three-stage fractionation protocol was subsequently established using these engineered MNPs in serial processing steps: first applying <90 nm-capture MNPs to remove the smallest EVs from biofluids, followed by <180 nm-capture MNPs to isolate medium-sized EVs, and concluding with >180 nm-capture MNPs to harvest large EVs, thereby achieving precise EV size fractionation (Fig. 1b). Each isolated EV subpopulation then underwent quantitative membrane protein analysis using a horseradish peroxidase (HRP)-based enzymatic signal amplification system, where HRP generated chemiluminescent (CL) signals proportional to specific biomarker on EV surfaces (Fig. 1c). The complete workflow was subsequently miniaturized into an integrated microfluidic system combining three essential components: (1) programmable peristaltic pumps for automated fluid handling, (2) microchannels implementing the sequential MNP processing steps, and (3) smartphone-based optical detectors for biomarker quantification, collectively enabling point-of-care clinical plasma analysis with a total processing time under 45 min (Fig. 1d). When applied to ICH diagnostics, this platform effectively discriminated size-subtype-specific EV protein signatures between ICH and IS patients through machine learning-assisted pattern recognition, demonstrating superior diagnostic performance compared to conventional approaches (Fig. 1e).

Steric hindrance-mediated size selective capture
Quantitative assessment of APT binding efficiency was performed through analysis of colorimetric ELISA signal variations under different experimental conditions (Fig. 2a). To minimize interference from MNP size heterogeneity, monodisperse MNPs with a controlled diameter of 37.8 ± 1.7 nm were employed throughout the study (Supplementary Fig. 1). APT and PEG were anchored at MNP surface through sequential aza-Michael addition (Supplementary Fig. 2) to give MNP decorated solely with APT (MNP-APT), solely with PEG (MNP-PEG), or with both APT and PEG (MNP-APT-PEG). The APT grafting ratio and PEG molecular weight of MNP-APT-PEG were designated as MNP-APT20%-PEG20K, where 20% denoted the APT grafting ratio and 20K denoted the PEG molecular weight (Mw = 20 kDa). Mesoporous silica nanoparticle (MSN), characterized by tunable nanoarchitectures, narrow size distributions, and low buoyant density34,35, served as synthetic EV analogues. Considering the established biological significance of 30 - 180 nm EV subpopulations in disease biomarker transport36,37, six distinct MSN size variants (37.5 nm, 61.1 nm, 93.1 nm, 124.1 nm, 152.7 nm, 182.9 nm) were functionalized with complementary sequence of APT (cAPT) and HRP (MSN-cAPT-HRP, Supplementary Fig. 3 and Fig. 4). The hybridization efficiency between surface-immobilized APT and cAPT served as the primary metric for binding efficiency quantification, as both DNA duplex formation and aptamer-protein recognition require complete spatial accessibility of aptamer sequences. PEG's inert chain effect was validated through statistically indistinguishable ELISA signals observed in MSN-cAPT-HRP solutions treated with PBS, MNP-PEG8K, MNP-PEG14K, and MNP-PEG20K (Supplementary Fig. 5a). Kinetic analysis demonstrated complete MSN capture within 30 min, as shown by time-dependent attenuation of ELISA signal difference before and after incubation with MNP-APT20%-PEG20K and MNP-APT40%-PEG20K (Supplementary Fig. 5b). High-resolution X-ray photoelectron spectroscope (XPS) analyses of C 1s, N 1s, and P 2p enabled precise calculation of APT grafting ratio (Supplementary Fig. 6). Fig. 2b demonstrated the APT grafting ratios increased from approximately 15% to 70% as the feeding ratios of APT were increased from 20% to 80%, confirming controllable aptamer surface functionalization

APT binding efficiency exhibited progressive reduction with decreasing aptamer grafting ratios, demonstrating pronounced attenuation at 40% and 20% grafting ratios (Fig. 2c). Under fixed 20% APT grafting ratio, MNPs functionalized with PEG having a molecular weight of 8 kDa, 10 kDa, and 12 kDa displayed marginal binding efficiency reductions compared to MNP-APT (PEG0K). Given APT 's molecular weight of 8,259.4 g/mol, this observation indicate subcritical steric hindrance when PEG chain length approximated or slightly exceeded the aptamer. A marked efficiency decline occurred in PEG14K, with progressive attenuation continuing until PEG chains molecular weight surpassed 20 kDa, beyond which binding efficiency plateaued at baseline levels (Fig. 2d). These data established that PEG polymers exceeding 14 kDa could generate sufficient steric barrier to effectively block APT -cAPT hybridization.

To establish MNP-APT-PEG systems with defined upper diameter thresholds for MSN-cAPT-HRP capture, systematic binding efficiency analyses were conducted using low APT grafting ratio (20% and 40%) and long PEG chain (Mw = 14 - 20 kDa) co-functionalized MNPs. Progressive reductions in binding efficiency were observed against MSN-cAPT-HRP with increasing diameters (Fig. 2e and 2f), confirming enhanced steric hindrance from cAPT at larger MSN surface. At 40% grafting ratio, APT retained measurable binding efficiencies (≥ 4%) across all MSN-cAPT-HRP diameters and PEG molecular weights (Fig. 2e). This residual activity stemmed from APT -saturated microdomains on MNP surface that preserved spatially confined hybridization zones. In contrast, MNPs with 20% APT grafting ratio exhibited <0.5% binding efficiency against 182.9 nm MSN-cAPT-HRP across all PEG variants, while MNP-APT20%-PEG20K showed equivalent suppression against MSNs exceeding 93.1 nm (Fig. 2f). Notably, MNP-APT20%-PEG20K retained strong binding against sub-93.1 nm MSNs, and MNP-APT20%-PEG14K demonstrated comparable performance for sub-182.9 nm MSNs, establishing capturable upper diameter limits of 93.1 nm and 182.9 nm, respectively. Consequently, MNP-APT20%-PEG20K and MNP-APT20%-PEG14K were employed to sequentially isolate MSNs with diameters <93.1 nm and those between 93.1 - 182.9 nm. To validate this separation capability, differentially sized MSN-cAPT-HRP particles (61.1 nm, 124.1 nm, and 182.9 nm) were fluorescently tagged with 7-Amino-4-methyl-3-coumarinylacetic acid N-succinimidyl ester (AMCA-NHS), fluorescein 5-isothiocyanate (FITC), and rhodamine B isothiocyanate (RITC), respectively. The labeled particles were mixed and subjected to sequential treatment with MNP-APT20%-PEG20K, followed by MNP-APT20%-PEG14K, and finally MNP-APT. This procedure resulted in the progressive disappearance of AMCA, FITC, and RITC fluorescence peaks from the residual mixture, accompanied by the emergence of corresponding fluorescence peaks with matching intensities in the isolated MSN fractions (Fig. 2g). The ordered elimination of AMCA, FITC, and RITC signals conclusively demonstrated the sequential isolation of 61.1 nm, 124.1 nm, and 182.9 nm MSNs by MNP-APT20%-PEG20K, MNP-APT20%-PEG14K, and MNP-APT, respectively.

Steric hindrance-mediated EV size fractionation
For EV size fractionation, MNP-APT20%-PEG20K, MNP-APT20%-PEG14K, and MNP-APT were sequentially applied to process EV containing solution. The concentration and purity of ultracentrifugation-isolated EVs were verified through nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA), transmission electron microscope (TEM), and western blotting (Supplementary Fig. 7). Prior to dynamic light scattering (DLS) and TEM characterization, EVs isolated via magnetic separation were chemically detached from MNPs using 10 mM dithiothreitol38. DLS measurements revealed mean hydrodynamic diameters of 54.4 ± 11.9 nm for EV subtype 1 and 127.9 ± 17.1 nm for EV subtype 2 (Fig. 3a), with corresponding size distributions spanning 23.8 - 86.5 nm (subtype 1) and 87.9 - 186.4 nm (subtype 2). These results confirmed that MNP-APT20%-PEG20K and MNP-APT20%-PEG14K maintained consistent size-selective performance for both synthetic MSNs and biological EVs. Residual nanostructures in EV subtype 3 (isolated by MNP-APT) exhibited a mean diameter of 220.2 ± 26.3 nm with a size distribution of 180.0 - 280.5 nm, demonstrating effective removal of sub-182.9 nm nanostructures during preceding fractionation steps. TEM analysis of the original EV solution revealed characteristic nano-vesicular structures exhibiting high-contrast peripheral membranes and electron-lucent compartments, with a mean diameter of 114.8 ± 38.0 nm (Fig. 3b, Input). Analogous vesicular morphologies were preserved across all fractionated EV subtypes: EV subtype 1 (56.8 ± 15.4 nm), EV subtype 2 (112.6 ± 6.4 nm), and EV subtype 3 (200.4 ± 20.2 nm), as investigated through systematic TEM measurements. This size-stratified conservation of structural features conclusively validated successful EV subtypes isolation via the steric hindrance-mediated methodology. Western blotting further confirmed subtype purity, with bands for EV biomarkers: CD63, heat shock proteins 70 (HSP70), ALG-2-interacting protein X (ALIX) detected in all size subtypes, while absent signals for apolipoprotein B (APOB) excluded plasma protein contamination across all subtypes (Fig. 3c). Note that the successful fractionation of the three EV subtypes was also validated by analyzing the TEM images of MNP-EV hybrid obtained through magnetic separation (Supplementary Fig. 8)

Three distinct EV size subtypes with diameters <90 nm, 90 - 180 nm, and >180 nm were successfully isolated from HUVEC, HMC3, SK-N-BE(2), and THP-1 cell culture mediums using steric hindrance-mediated fractionation (Supplementary Fig. 9), validating the method's efficacy across diverse cellular origins. A strong linear correlation (R2 = 0.9079) was observed between EV protein concentrations from steric hindrance-isolated subtypes and NTA-quantified particle concentrations (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Fig. 10), confirming high size-fractionation accuracy and specificity. Notably, EV subtype 2 (90–180 nm) showed higher abundance compared to the other two subtypes across all four cell lines, consistent with published data and attributable to inherent EV biogenesis characteristics. The 90–180 nm range encompasses fractions of two major EV subpopulations: large EVs (100–1000 nm) generated by plasma membrane budding, and exosomes (< 200 nm) derived from the endosomal pathway39,40. Total EV recovery rates exceeded 95% at EV concentrations ≤1.0×1012 particle/mL, with <5% inter-subtype variability across solutions of varying EV concentrations (Fig. 3e). However, at 5×1012 particle/mL, a significant recovery rate elevation occurred specifically in subtype 3, revealing incomplete isolation of sub-180 nm EVs by MNP-APT20%-PEG20K and MNP-APT20%-PEG14K. This delineated the method's operational upper limit at 1×1012 particle/mL, consistent with clinically relevant EV concentrations (sub-1×1012 particle/mL) observed in plasma from stroke or cancer patients41,42.

The SHEAF platform offers significant advantages over established EV fractionation methods, such as size exclusion chromatography (SEC), density gradient ultracentrifugation (DGUC) and asymmetric-flow field-flow fractionation (AF4). Using a self-made SEC column, EVs in native biofluids were separated into three size fractions (<50 nm, 110 nm, and 210 nm) within 1 h (Fig. 3f upper)27,43-45. However, the SEC method had limited EV recovery (65.53%) and substantial protein contamination in the <50 nm fraction (Fig. 3g left and 3 h left). Per established protocols, DGUC requires 12-hour ultracentrifugation to accelerate particle movement through density gradient flotation, plus pre- and post-fractionation ultracentrifugation to remove protein contaminants46-48. Our results confirmed DGUC exhibited poor size resolution due to overlapping EV densities (Fig. 3f lower)46 and APOB contamination issues in FS7 (Fig. 3g right). Additionally, DGUC demonstrated a low EV recovery rate of only 71.33% (Fig. 3h right), attributed in part to EV membrane rupture during the high-speed ultracentrifugation48,49. AF4, a recently developed microfluidic EV fractionation method, was reported to provide high size resolution but require pre-processing with ultracentrifugation (2 h) to remove protein aggregations, limiting its clinical utility25,50. Overall, SHEAF can separate EV in complex biofluids into three high-purity EV size subtypes in 1 h without pre-processing, achieving near-complete recovery (>95%) and minimal protein contamination (Supplementary Table 1).

Molecular profiling of EV size subtypes
The SHEAF platform was employed to analyze EV membrane proteins across three EV size subtypes secreted by HUVEC and HMC3. Cells were stimulated with tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNF-α) or oxidized low-density lipoprotein (OX-LDL) to establish inflammatory models prior to medium collection (Supplementary Fig. 11). Six inflammation-related proteins, including vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β), programmed cell death ligand 1 (PD-L1), C-reactive protein (CRP), TNF-α, and intercellular adhesion molecule 1 (ICAM-1), were selected for analysis based on their known associations with EV membrane and elevated circulatory levels in stroke patients51-56. EV membrane proteins were first labeled via double-stranded DNA comprising an aptamer sequence against target protein and an HRP-conjugated transducing sequence (APT -TR -HRP). Activating sequence (ACT ) subsequently displaced TR -HRP from EV surfaces within 30 min, initiating the CL reaction through interaction with ELISA substrate. This HRP-catalyzed system demonstrated target-specific membrane protein recognition, evidenced by substantially amplified CL signals in EV solutions treated with APT -TR -HRP plus ACT (Fig. 4a). By contrast, negligible signal enhancement occurred when APT -TR -HRP was replaced with its scrambled sequence counterpart or when EV solutions were treated solely with APT -TR -HPR or ACT (PBS). The steric hindrance-mediated EV size fractionation technique and membrane protein analysis workflow were subsequently incorporated into a microfluidic platform, which achieved a VEGF detection limit of 0.380 × 107 particle/mL during titration experiments on VEGF associated to HMC3 EV membrane (Fig. 4b).

Expression levels of the six proteins in the whole EV population were quantified using both the SHEAF platform and sandwich ELISA for comparative analysis. SHEAF-derived measurements showed strong linear correlation with ELISA results (R2 = 0.9682, Fig. 4c), confirming method reliability. Subsequent analysis revealed distinct protein expression patterns across all three EV subtypes in various inflammation models. Specifically, elevated signals were observed in EV subtype 1 and EV subtype 2 compared to whole EV population and EV subtype 3 (Fig. 4d), demonstrating inflammation-related protein enrichment in these subtypes. Pairwise comparisons of EV membrane protein compositions were further used to evaluate the correlations between the three EV size subtypes and whole EV population. Positive correlations were detected between nearly all EV size subtypes and the whole EV population, given their shared common cellular origins (Fig. 4e). However, weak correlations or negative correlations (r ≤ 0.1) were identified between EV subtype 1 and EV subtype 2 derived from HMC3 cells, along with EV subtype 2 and EV subtype 3 isolated from TNF-α stimulated HUVEC cultures. Furthermore, moderate correlations (0.1 <r ≤0.5) were observed between EV subtype 3 and two other EV subtypes in OX-LDL-stimulated HUVECs, and with EV subtype 2 in TNF-α-stimulated HMC3 cells. These weak inter-subtype correlations revealed substantial biomolecular and biophysical heterogeneity intrinsic to EVs, thereby emphasizing the indispensable requirement for sophisticated EV size subtype methodologies in elucidating EV-associated biological mechanisms. Proteomic analysis further delineated distinct protein expression profiles among the three EV subtypes (Supplementary Fig. 12a,b). Analysis of the proteomic dataset for subcellular localization indicated that the proteins significantly enriched in EV Subtype 2 were derived from diverse intracellular compartments (Supplementary Fig. 12c,d), suggesting this subtype is likely produced mainly through the endosomal pathway. This origin underpinned its enhanced potential as a source of diagnostic biomarkers. Notably, proteins detected by western blotting were also identified within the proteomic dataset.

Clinical sample analysis
To assess the diagnostic efficacy of the SHEAF platform for stroke classification, plasma samples were collected from 25 ICH patients and 25 IS patients. In addition, plasma samples from 20 healthy donors were collected through age- and sex-matched cohort enrollment as control group (Supplementary Table 2). Employing the SHEAF platform, EVs in patient plasma samples were categorized into 3 size subtypes (Supplementary Fig. 13), followed by membrane protein profiling for both fractionated EVs and whole EV population. Substantial disparities in expression levels were detected among the six target proteins when comparing the three EV size subtypes with whole EV population (Fig. 5a). This finding was consistent with the cellular analysis, thereby reinforcing the functional specialization of EV subtypes in inflammatory pathway regulation.

Two-dimensional projections of EV protein compositions across three size subtypes and the whole EV population were generated through principal component analysis (PCA). Significant spatial overlap was identified between ICH, IS, and healthy cohorts in the protein profiles of EV subtype 1, subtype 3, and the unfractionated EV pool (Fig. 5b). Conversely, EV subtype 2 demonstrated minimal inter-group overlap in protein composition. This differential clustering pattern suggested superior diagnostic capability of EV subtype 2 protein signatures for distinguishing stroke from healthy control and ICH from IS. Consistent with PCA findings, EV subtypes 1, subtype 3, and whole EVs demonstrated limited ability to differentiate between stroke and healthy plasma samples, and between ICH and IS samples (Supplementary Fig. 14). The mixed area under the curve (AUC) scores for these populations were 0.807 (subtype 1), 0.695 (subtype 3), and 0.792 (whole EVs) in distinguishing stroke from healthy controls, with most individual protein AUC values below 0.70. For differentiating ICH from IS, the mixed AUCs were 0.728 (subtype 1), 0.680 (subtype 3), and 0.736 (whole EVs), again with most individual protein AUCs below 0.60. In contrast, proteins from EV subtype 2 showed markedly improved diagnostic performance in both comparisons (Fig. 5c, upper). Specifically, TGF-β and PD-L1 achieved AUC values above 0.80 for distinguishing stroke from healthy controls, while a combined six-protein panel in subtype 2 yielded an exceptional AUC of 0.951 in stroke diagnosis. Similarly, in differentiating ICH from IS, all individual proteins in subtype 2 had AUC values exceeding 0.60, with VEGF, CRP, and ICAM-1 surpassing 0.70 (Fig. 5c, lower). The combined model based on EV subtype 2 reached an AUC of 0.958 for classifying ICH versus IS. The cut-points for EV subtype 2 showed a sensitivity of 0.88 and a specificity of 0.92 in differentiating ICH from IS, as well as a sensitivity of 0.84 and a specificity of 0.95 in distinguishing stroke from healthy controls (Supplementary Table 3).

---

## Methods

Materials
DNA oligos were purchased from Sangon Biotech (Shanghai) Co., Ltd. and were stored at -20 oC before use. Aptamer sequences against CD63, VEGF, TGF-β, PD-L1, CRP, TNF-α, and ICAM-1 were established according to previous publications (Supplementary Table 5)60-65. Primary amine capped MNP (MNP-NH ) and OptiPrep™ density gradient medium (60%, w/v, iodixanol) were obtained from Merck Ltd. TNF-α, OX-LDL, SuperSignal™ ELISA Femto substrate, HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody (Invitrogen, catalog no. A16066), and primary antibodies against the following proteins - CD63 (Invitrogen, clone Mo34, catalog no. MA5-47655), HSP70 (Invitrogen, clone 2A4, catalog no. MA3-008), ALIX (Invitrogen, clone 3A9, catalog no. MA1-83977), APOB (NeoBiotechnologies, clone APOB/4335, catalog no. 338-MSM5-P1) - were purchased from Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc. Diacrylate PEG (DAPEG, Mw = 1,000), methoxypolyethylene glycol amine (mPEG-NH , Mw = 8,000, 10,000, 20,000 and 30,000), PEG bis(amine) (NH -PEG-NH , Mw = 2,000, 4,000, 6,000 and 8,000), PEG methyl ether acrylate (PEG-MA, Mw = 10,000 and 20,000), triethylamine, and N,N-methylenediacrylamide were purchased from Beijing InnoChem Science & Technology Co., Ltd. AMCA-NHS, FITC, RITC, tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS), (3-aminopropyl)triethoxysilane (APTES), hexadecyltrimethylammonium bromide (CTAB), and polyetherimide (PEI, Mw = 600) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin BioChem Technology Co., Ltd, and were used as received. Sepharose® CL-2B agarose gel, ELISA for IL-1β and MCP-1, bicinchoninic acid assay (BCA), radioimmunoprecipitation assay (RIPA) containing protease inhibitors, HRP streptavidin, TMB single-component substrate solution, and ELISA stopping solution were purchased from Shanghai Acmec Biochemical Co., Ltd. EV-depleted fetal bovine serum were prepared according to standard protocol49.

Cell culture and EV collection
HUVEC (catalog no. GPC0114) cell line was purchased from the China Center for Type Culture Collection (Wuhan, China). HMC3 (catalog no. SCSP-540), SK-N-BE(2) (catalog no. TCHu200), and THP-1 (catalog no. SCSP-567) cell lines were purchased from the National Collection of Authenticated Cell Cultures (Shanghai, China). All cell lines were cultured in Dulbecco`s modified Eagle`s medium (DMEM, Gibco) containing 10% EV-depleted fetal bovine serum and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco). After being cultured for 48 h, the cell culture mediums were centrifuged at 1,000 g for 20 min and treated by a 0.22 μm filter. The obtained supernatant was sequentially centrifuged at 10,000 g for 10 min and 100,000 g for 90 min to isolate EV. The EV pellet was washed by resuspending in PBS and centrifugation at 100,000 g for 90 min.
For analyzing EV secreted by cells under inflammatory states, HUVEC and HMC3 cells were exposed to TNF-α or OX-LDL according to previous publications66-68. In a typical procedure, 1.0  106 HMC3 cells were incubated with 100 ng/mL TNF-α or 50 μg/mL OX-LDL for 24 h before collecting cell culture mediums. Cellular inflammatory models were validated by measuring inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β and MCP-1) levels in cell culture mediums via ELISA per the manufacturer’s protocol. The harvested EVs were investigated by western blotting, NTA, and TEM to confirm their protein composition, concentration, and structure, respectively. To preserve EV integrity, disaggregation was not performed during the EV isolation step.

Surface modification of MNP-NH
In a typical procedure, 0.5 mg MNP-NH and 10 mg DAPEG were incubated together in 1.0 mL PBS for 24 h at 37 oC. The obtained MNP-DAPEG was further incubated with APT (2.0 μM, primary amine at 5` end) and mPEG-NH (8.0 μM, Mw = 20,000) for 24 h to obtain MNP with 20% APT grafting ratio (MNP-APT20%-PEG20K). The APT grafting ratio of MNP was adjusted by varying the dosage of APT and mPEG-NH . After each step, the MNP was dialyzed (MWCO = 50,000) against PBS for 24 h to remove residuals. The MNP surface modification process was illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 2.
mPEG-NH with molecular weight of 8,000, 10,000, 20,000, and 30,000 were commercially available and directly used in MNP surface modification. mPEG-NH with molecular weight of 12,000, 14,000, 16,000, 18,000 and 24,000 were synthesized through aza-Michael reaction. Typically, 1.0 mg PEG-MA (Mw = 10,000) and 10 mg NH -PEG-NH (Mw = 2,000) were added into 2.0 mL PBS and reacted at 37 oC for 24 h. Then, the mixture was treated by a dialysis bag (MWCO = 5,000) against PBS for 48 h, followed by lyophilization to give mPEG-NH with a Mw of 12,000.

Preparation and surface modification of MSN
Primary amine capped MSN (MSN-NH ) were prepared according to previous publications34,35. Briefly, 0.4 g APTES and 1.6 g TEOS were mixed and slowly added into 140 mL CTAB solution (4.0 mM). Then, 0.5 mL NH3•H2O (30%) was added into the mixture under stirring, followed by reacting at 25 oC for 5 h. Subsequently, the obtained solid was collected by centrifugation and washed with ethanol. To remove residual CTAB, the obtained MSN-NH was treated by 100 mL HCl solution (3.7%) for 12 h at 60 oC. To control the size of MSN-NH , the dosage of silane and NH3•H2O were adjusted.
For labeling MSN with HRP and cAPT (primary amine at 5` end), 1.0 mg MSN-NH and 10.0 mg N,N-methylenediacrylamide were incubated in 1.0 mL PBS buffer at 37 oC for 24 h. After being washed by centrifugation and re-dispersion, the solution was further incubated with 100 μL mixture solution containing HRP (1.0 mg/mL) and cAPT (100 μM, primary amine at 5` end) for 24 h at 37 oC. The obtained MSN-cAPT-HRP was purified by centrifugation and re-dispersing in PBS. In a typical procedure for labeling MSN with fluorophores, 1.0 mL MSN-cAPT-HRP (1.0 mg/mL) was reacted with 0.5 mg FITC for 12 h at 25 oC in dark. Then, the FITC labeled MSN was purified by centrifugation and re-dispersion in PBS. The MSN surface modification process was illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 4.

APT binding efficiency investigation
The binding efficiency of APT at MNP surface was investigated by analyzing the amount of MSN-cAPT-HRP remained in the solution after being treated by MNP-APT-PEG. In a typical procedure, 50 μL MSN-cAPT-HRP solution (diameter = 124.1 nm, 0.01 mg/mL) was incubated with 50 μL MNP-APT20%-PEG20K solution (0.1 mg/mL) for 30 min at 25 oC. Steric hindrance mediated EV size fractionation
In the first round of EV size fractionation process, 10 μL MNP-APT20%-PEG20K (0.5 mg/mL) solution was incubated with 40 μL EV containing medium for 30 min at 25 oC. Then, the mixture was treated by a magnetic bar for 3 min to collect EV subtype 1 (EV diameter <90 nm). The EV containing supernatant was further treated by 10 μL MNP-APT20%-PEG14K (0.5 mg/mL) and a magnetic bar under the same procedure to collect EV subtype 2 (90 nm <EV diameter <180 nm). Finally, the EVs remained in the supernatant were treated by 10 μL MNP-APT (0.5 mg/mL) and a magnetic bar to harvest EV subtype 3 (180 nm <EV diameter). Prior to size fractionating, all EV containing mediums were treated by 0.22 μm filters. For analyzing the morphology and size of each EV subtype, cystamine was conjugated to the 5` end of APT before it was decorated to MNP surface. After fractionating, EV and MNP mixtures were treated by 10 mM dithiothreitol for 4 h at 37 oC to release EV from MNP surface for measuring hydrodynamic size by a DLS instrument38.

EV membrane protein profiling
The expression levels of EV membrane associated proteins, including VEGF, TGF-β, PD-L1, CRP, TNF-α, and ICAM-1, were analyzed by an HRP catalyzed CL reaction. Typically, APT was hybridized with TR -HRP to obtain APT -TR -HRP. Then, 5 μL APT -TR -HRP (1.0 μg/mL) solution and 10 μL MNP-APT20%-PEG20K (0.5 mg/mL) solution were incubated together with 40 μL EV containing medium for 30 min, followed by the same EV size fractionation processes described in Section “Steric hindrance mediated EV size fractionation”. For each subtype, the MNP-EV hybrid was treated by ACT (30μL, 0.1 μM) for 30 min at 25 oC to detach TR -HRP from EV surface. Subsequently, the released TR -HRP were transferred and treated by SuperSignal™ ELISA Femto substrate to measure CL signal at 425 nm. The scrambled structure of APT -TR -HRP was used to treat the EV containing medium with the same procedure as negative control. The signals for protein measurement was defined as ∆CL and was calculated as:

where CL and CL were the CL signals of samples treated by aptamer sequence and scrambled sequence, respectively. The TR -HRP were prepared by incubating TR (biotin at 5` end) with HRP streptavidin at 25 oC for 4 h, followed by removing residual TR using a Zeba™ spin desalting column (Thermo, MWCO = 40,000).

Microfluidic chip fabrication
The microfluidic chip comprised three layers. The cover layer was fabricated from a PMMA sheet using a CO laser engraver (Atomstack K60). The microchannel layer was produced through SU-8 photolithography. Specifically, SU-8 photoresist was spin-coated onto a silicon wafer and UV-exposed to pattern a casting mold. A PDMS/crosslinker mixture (10:1) was poured onto this mold, cured at 60°C overnight, and then peeled off. Holes for the inlet and outlet ports were punched into the PDMS layer using a hole puncher. To covalently bond the layers together, the cover and substrate layers were surface-activated with oxygen plasma, followed by immersion in APTES solution (5% v/v) for 20 min. The microchannel layer was then surface-activated with oxygen plasma and attached to the cover and substrate layers overnight at 70°C. The fabrication processes and operational procedure of microfluidic chip were illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 15 and Fig. 16.

Device integration and manipulation
The pumping system consisted of four components: a peristaltic pump (Kamoer), a manifold with nine solenoid valves (Dehnker), a control board, and six electromagnets (JX-P10/10). This pumping system, along with three microfluidic chips and an optical detector, was assembled into a 3D-printed enclosure (Bambu Lab X1) to form the SHEAF platform, which was connected to a smartphone interface via Bluetooth. For the work-flow of the integrated SHEAF device, 10 μL plasma sample and 2.5 μL solution containing MNP-APT20%-PEG20K (0.5 mg/mL) and APT -TR -HRP (0.5 μg/mL) were introduced through inlet 1 and inlet 2, respectively. The mixture solution was directed through the serpentine channel into the incubation chamber, followed by incubating for 10 min and electromagnetic separation to isolate EV subtype1. The supernatant was transferred to the second microfluidic chip for isolating EV subtype 2 and the third microfluidic chip for isolating EV subtype 3 under the same protocol in a sequential manner. The obtained MNP-EV hybrid was mixed with 7.5 μL ACT (0.1 μM) solution introduced via inlet 3 and was incubated together in the next incubation chamber for 10 min to release TR -HRP. Then, the electromagnet was activated to sediment MNP-EV hybrid , while the TR -HRP was further mixed with 2.0 μL ELISA substrate introduced via inlet 4. The CL reaction was carried out for 120 s with the CL intensity being recorded by a smartphone. Plasma samples treated by the scrambled structure of APT -TR -HRP were used as negative control. The system configuration and operational logic of the SHEAF device were illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 17. The optimization and reproducibility of SHEAF device was illustrated in Supplementary Fig. 18.

Clinical samples
Clinical analyses were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the Helsinki Declaration and received approval from the Ethics Committee of Guizhou Medical University (Approval No. 2024-126). Informed consent was secured from each participant before blood samples collection. Clinical samples of stroke patients were collected at the Department of emergency of The Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou Medical University, while clinical samples of healthy controls were collected at the Department of Cardiovascular Medicine. The initial cohort of samples was collected from January to September 2024, while the additional samples incorporated during the revision phase were obtained between August and October 2025. Clinical diagnoses were performed by medical staff from the Department of Emergency Medicine and the Department of Cardiovascular Medicine. Subsequent analyses based on SHEAF platform were conducted by researchers from the School of Pharmacy at Guizhou Medical University and School of Mechanical Engineering at Northwestern Polytechnical University. All sample-related assays were performed in a blinded manner. For stroke patients, blood was collected prior to any treatment intervention. Diagnosis of either ICH or IS was confirmed within one hour after blood sampling. Prior to the study, none of the patients had a history of stroke or myocardial infarction, nor had they received any form of treatment for stroke. The baseline characteristics of patients were summarized in Supplementary Table 2.
Blood samples were collected in EDTA tubes, followed by immediate centrifugation at 1,000 g for 10 min to harvest upper plasma layer. The collected plasma was further centrifuged at 10,000 g for 10 min and was filtered through a 0.22 μm filter to remove large aggregations. Then, the plasma samples were stored at - 80 oC before use. A total of 70 samples were collected, including 25 patients with ICH, 25 patients with IS, and 20 healthy donors. The clinical diagnoses were made by neurologists following a series of clinical tests for each patient. These tests included physical and neurological examinations, blood tests, MRI, and computed CT scans. The clinical samples were analyzed by the integrated SHEAF platform according to work-flow described in Section “Device integration and manipulation”.

Western blotting
EVs were lysed by RIPA buffer and were quantified using BCA assay. Subsequently, the EV proteins were resolved by sodium dodecyl sulfate-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred onto a poly(vinylidene fluoride) membrane. After being washed by Tris buffered saline with Tween-20 and blocked with 5% skimmed milk, the blots were further incubated with primary antibodies against the following proteins: CD63, ALIX, HSP70, and APOB at 4 °C for 12 h. After incubation, the blots were washed and treated with an HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse IgG secondary antibody for 2 h. Finally, the CL of blot was analyzed using a BIORAD ChemiDOC™ XRS imaging system.

Proteomic analysis of EV size subtypes
EV size subtypes were fractionated using the SHEAF platform from the cell culture mediums of HUVEC and HMC3. Each EV size subtype was re-dispersed in PBS and treated with 1.0% Triton X-100 for 30 min at 37 oC, followed by magnetic separation to remove MNP. The obtained sample solution was further treated with lysis buffer (4% sodium dodecyl sulfate, 100 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.6) directly. Subsequently, dithiothreitol was added to each sample to reduce disulfide bonds by incubating at 37 oC for 1.5 h, followed by incubation with iodoacetamide for 30 min at 25 oC to block cysteine residues. Trypsin was added into sample solution at a trypsin-to-protein ratio of 1:50 (w/w), and the mixture was incubated at 37°C overnight. The digested peptides were desalted using an MCX desalting column (Omicsolution, OS-MCX-1ML), concentrated by vacuum centrifugation, and reconstituted in 20 μL formic acid solution (0.1%). The peptide concentration was estimated by measuring the UV absorbance at 280 nm. The obtained sample solution was mixed with iRT peptides (Biognosys) according to manufacturer`s guidance for data-independent acquisition (DIA) experiments.
Peptides from each sample were analyzed using an OrbitrapTM AstralTM mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific) coupled with a Vanquish Neo UHPLC system (Thermo Scientific) in DIA mode. MS1 spectra (intact form) were acquired over a mass range of 380–980 m/z with a resolution of 240,000 at 200 m/z, a normalized automatic gain control target of 500%, and a maximum injection time of 5 ms. MS2 (fragmented form) analysis was performed with 299 windows, an isolation window of 2 m/z, and an HCD collision energy of 25 eV, using a normalized automatic gain control target of 500% and a maximum injection time of 3 ms. The acquired data were processed with DIA-NN (version 1.8.1) using the following parameters: enzyme set to trypsin, maximum missed cleavages set to 1, fixed modification set to carbamidomethylation, and dynamic modifications set to oxidation and N-terminal acetylation. Subcellular localization of proteins was predicted using CELLO (http://cello.life.nctu.edu.tw/), a multi-class support vector machine-based classification system. All reported identifications were based on 99% confidence at the protein level, corresponding to a false discovery rate ≤ 1%.

EV size fractionation by SEC and DGUC
The SEC-based EV size fractionation was performed according to previous publications27,43. Sepharose® CL-2B agarose gel was mixed 3:1 (v/v) with PBS buffer and stacked into plastic columns (inner diameter 5 mm) to a height of 20 cm. The columns were equilibrated with 10 mL of PBS buffer for 30 min prior to the loading of 500 μL EV containing medium. The eluate collection was initiated immediately using graduated 2.0 mL glass tubes, yielding 300 μL per fraction. The presence and size distribution of EVs in each eluate were assessed by DLS analysis.
For DGUC-based EV size fraction, OptiPrep™ density gradient medium (60%, w/v, iodixanol) were diluted in cold PBS to give solutions with 40%, 20%, 10%, and 5% iodixanol46,47. Then, 2 mL of those iodixanol solutions each was gentle layered in an ultracentrifugation tube in descending order of concentration to generate a discontinuous density gradient. Crude EV pellet isolated by ultracentrifugation was placed at the bottom of the tube. The bottom-loaded 5% - 40% gradient was centrifuged at 100,000 g for 12 h at 4 oC. After ultracentrifugation, 8 fractions (1 mL each) were collected from the top of the gradient, followed by resuspension in PBS and ultracentrifugation at 100,000 g for 90 min at oC. The obtained pellet was resuspended in PBS for further analysis.

Instrument
The solution absorbance, fluorescence, and CL measurements were performed on a plate reader (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 25 oC. The hydration diameters (number average) and surface zeta potentials of EVs were analyzed by a DLS instrument (NanoBrook 173Plus, Brookhaven) at 25 oC. The concentration of the isolated EV was determined using an NTA system (ZetaView, Particle Metrix) in PBS buffer at 25 oC. For each NTA analysis, 11 positions were recorded using a maximum area of 1000, a minimum area of 10, and a minimum brightness of 30. TEM images were acquired using a TalosTM L120C G2 (Thermo) instrument operated at an accelerating voltage of 120 kV. EV size subtypes were visualized without staining, while EV-MNP hybrids were visualized after staining with phosphotungstic acid to enhance the contrast of EVs. The morphology and size of MSN-NH were analyzed by a scanning electron microscope (CLARA S-3400N, TESCAN). MSN-NH was dispersed on a silica wafer and subjected to 60 s of gold sputter-coating prior to SEM analysis. XPS analysis was performed on an ESXCALAB Xi+ instrument (Thermo), and data was analyzed by Thermo Scientific™ Avantage software. The ultracentrifugation was performed by an Optima XPN (Beckman) at 4 oC. A SW 41 Ti rotor (Beckman, k factor = 124) and Thinwall Polyallomer tubes (Beckman) were employed for this procedure.

Statistics
All experiments were conducted in triplicate unless otherwise specified, and the results were presented as the mean ± standard deviation (SD). Experiments were repeated thrice independently with similar results for Figs. 3b, c, g. P <0.05 was considered the threshold for statistical significance. Pairwise correlation analysis (Pearson) was employed to generate correlation matrices for EV membrane proteins. False discovery rate was used to assess the proportion of false positives in multiple hypothesis testing. Sample size calculation were performed with α = 0.05 and power (1 – β) = 0.95. The calculated false discovery rate and sample size were summarized in Supplementary Table 6. The EV membrane protein expression levels of clinical samples were visualized in a two-dimensional space using PCA. ## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript, Zhao et al. describe a microfluidic platform (termed SHEAF) that integrates steric-hindrance-mediated magnetic sorting of plasma extracellular vesicles (EVs) with chemiluminescent membrane-protein profiling to achieve rapid, pre-hospital discrimination of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) from ischemic stroke (IS). The authors report that the 90–180 nm EV subtype (subtype 2) exhibits superior discriminative capacity in differentiating ICH from IS within a 45-min workflow. Although the technical ingenuity and potential clinical impact are compelling, several concerns need to be addressed before the work can be recommended for publication:
1. The authors use 90 nm and 180 nm as cut-offs, yet the rationale is lacking (Fig. 2f). Please clarify why these diameters are biologically meaningful for stroke-related EVs. It seems that the abundance of the 90–180 nm subtype 2 is much higher than subtype 1 and 3.
2. How the PEG layer generates a steric barrier: relate PEG length (14–20 kDa) to the resulting exclusion distance. Will PEG steric hindrance compromise the recognition ability of aptamers? Why use aptamers instead of antibodies?
3. Provide large-area TEM micrographs that show intact EVs bound to MNPs for all three size fractions.
4. Please include NTA. TEM, and Western-blot data for the three size subtypes isolated from plasma samples.
5. Clarify why VEGF, TGF-β, PD-L1, CRP, TNF-α, and ICAM-1 were chosen.
6. Explain mechanistically why subtype 2 (90–180 nm) is diagnostically superior.
7. Please add more clinical samples and include healthy controls.

### Reviewer 2

Noteworthy and significance:
The new method presented in this paper is of scientific merit and clearly based upon well established ideas for nanoparticle and filtration based techniques. The authors propose a rapid method for the detection of three EV subtypes based upon their preliminary research.
The technique offers a high purity EV recovery (95%), this will be particularly interesting to the EV community. Integration into a microfluidic device offers a unique, dedicated apparatus for EV isolation. The use of smart phone detection is innovative but should be treated cautiously.
Conclusions:
The authors offer significant support in the manuscript to support their ideas. They validated using multiple gold standard techniques and provided tangible evidence (TEM, NTP and Western blotting). Many of their ideas are supported with the literature such as EVs carrying proinflammatory markers.
Additional evidence and flaws:
The author have not stated the properties of these EV subtypes other than size or vesicle diameter, however there are distinct subtypes of EV that are produced with distinctive sizes that are formed through different biogenic pathways.
These have characteristic biomarkers, such as sMVs or exosomes typically express CD63 on their outer membrane and are 30 - 100nm (there abouts) and are as a result of the endocytic pathway, however, microvesicles (s/EVs) are larger 100nmm - 1000nm, produced by blebbing at the cell surface and express little or no CD63. From what I can ascertain, there are two populations of microvesicles, that should express negligible CD63 levels.
Is it possible that the fractions containing larger EVs are 'contaminated' with smaller, aggregated EVs expressing CD63? I saw no comment about disaggregation steps in the protocols.
Conceptually the work is interesting and if correct will offer an advantage to clinical laboratories.
I would urge the authors to address this in their manuscript, either highlighting this as a flaw, altering their emphasis and conclusions or addressing this issue with the necessary supportive supplementary information, i.e., that they have removed aggregated exosomes, that the cells themselves express CD63 on their surface or that all EV subtypes are enriched for CD63 - this is highly unlikely though.
The clinical sample size is relatively small. Although a larger sample size is probably difficult to find participants the authors should acknowledge this as a limitation or propose a larger study.
Methods:
This are sounds - except what has been previously stated. Gold standard tools are used.
The methods should be reproducible based upon protocol written, including aptimer sequences and analytical techniques and so on.
However, the manufacture and calibration of the microfluidic device requires more detail.
Overall, the work is exciting and conducted well. It has the potential to offer a clear clinical application as well as offering a rapid techniques for research labs too.
Addressing my comments will strengthen the overall impact of the manuscript.

### Reviewer 3

In this manuscript entitled “Steric Hindrance-Mediated Extracellular Vesicle Size Fractionation for Rapid Prehospital Diagnosis of Intracerebral Hemorrhage”, the authors present a novel SHEAF platform designed to enable rapid EV size-fractionation and protein profiling. They report that EVs within the 90–180 nm range demonstrate potential as highly discriminative biomarkers for ICH, with possible applications for rapid and precise stroke diagnostics in the prehospital setting.
The paper is clearly written, and the investigators provide interesting and timely data. Nonetheless, several important aspects require clarification and further elaboration. My detailed comments are outlined below.
- The introduction is overly superficial. Relevant issues such as cause-specific management of acute stroke patients in the prehospital setting (e.g., blood pressure control and the need for ICH patients to be admitted to specialized units) are not addressed. A more comprehensive rationale for the study design is required, particularly concerning the potential added value of including EVs. Additionally, the cited literature is somewhat outdated.
- The methodological section is insufficiently detailed. Critical clinical information is missing, such as patient recruitment details (e.g., location, timeframe), laboratory where analyses were performed, and whether assays were conducted in a blinded manner. The timing of sample collection—fundamental to the claimed prehospital application—is not reported. The statistical methods are inadequately described, with no mention of sample size calculation, limited descriptive statistics, and no adjustment for multiple comparisons.
- The absence of a healthy control group significantly weakens the interpretability of the findings.
- The claim that the platform could serve as a robust prehospital diagnostic system is unrealistic. The requirement for plasma processing and the reported 45-minute workflow make its use in ambulances unfeasible.
- The statement that the platform outperforms “conventional approaches” is vague, as no clear comparator methods are identified.
- Several claims lack statistical support. For example, differences in protein expression levels across EV subtypes (Fig. 5a) are not substantiated by statistical testing. Results of the multiple linear regression models for stroke diagnosis are not reported. ROC analyses raise concerns given the small sample size, and in subtype 2, the majority of proteins demonstrate only poor discriminatory power (AUC 0.6–0.7). Furthermore, 95% confidence intervals—essential to quantify uncertainty—are not provided. The statement that subtype 2 achieved “near-ideal classification accuracy” (AUC 0.933) is overstated, especially since no cut-offs, sensitivity, or specificity are provided.
- The discussion does not sufficiently address the biological or pathophysiological rationale underlying the superior performance of subtype 2 EVs. Moreover, there is no consideration of the optimal diagnostic time window for the proposed approach.
- The limitations of the study are not adequately acknowledged, including small sample size, lack of control for confounders (e.g., age, sex, comorbidities), absence of healthy controls, and missing sampling time points—all of which preclude meaningful conclusions about prehospital applicability.

Point-by-point response
Reviewer #1:
In this manuscript, Zhao et al. describe a microfluidic platform (termed SHEAF) that
integrates steric-hindrance-mediated magnetic sorting of plasma extracellular vesicles
(EVs) with chemiluminescent membrane-protein profiling to achieve rapid, pre-hospital
discrimination of intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) from ischemic stroke (IS). The authors
report that the 90–180 nm EV subtype (subtype 2) exhibits superior discriminative capacity
in differentiating ICH from IS within a 45-min workflow. Although the technical ingenuity and
potential clinical impact are compelling, several concerns need to be addressed before the
work can be recommended for publication:
1. The authors use 90 nm and 180 nm as cut-offs, yet the rationale is lacking (Fig. 2f).
Please clarify why these diameters are biologically meaningful for stroke-related EVs. It
seems that the abundance of the 90–180 nm subtype 2 is much higher than subtype 1 and
3.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. Extracellular vesicles
(EVs) below approximately 200 nm are known to cross the blood-brain barrier (BBB),
making them ideal candidates for detecting brain-specific changes in the early phases of
stroke1-3. Furthermore, EVs smaller than 90 nm possess limited membrane surface area
for adequately displaying stroke-specific biomarkers4, while those exceeding 200 nm may
include heterogeneous apoptotic bodies. Thus, the 90–180 nm range represents an
optimal balance: it enriches for brain-derived EVs with sufficient surface area to carry
disease-relevant proteins, while minimizing inclusion of larger heterogenous particles.
Supporting this, our proteomic analysis revealed that EV subtype 2 (90–180 nm) contains
a significantly greater number of proteins of subcellular origin compared to subtype 1
(<90 nm) and subtype 3 (>180 nm), further underscoring the critical importance of
subtype 2 as a diagnostically relevant EV fraction enriched in intracellular, and potentially
brain-specific, biomarkers (new Supplementary Figure 12).
Although biologically informed, the exact thresholds of 90 nm and 180 nm were determined
empirically based on the binding behavior of aptamer- and PEG-functionalized magnetic
nanoparticles (MNPs). Through systematical investigation (Figure 2), we observed two
MNP formulations selectively bound nanoparticles below approximately 182.9 nm and
93.1 nm, respectively, while effectively shielding larger particles. These two MNP
formulations were subsequently applied in EV size fractionation for selectively capture EV
below 90 nm and 180 nm, respectively.
Our experimental data, derived from both bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay and nanoparticle
tracking analyzer (NTA), indicate much higher abundance of EVs within the 90–180 nm
size range (subtype 2). This observation aligns with previously published reports5,6, and
can be attributed to the inherent characteristics of EV biogenesis. Specifically, EVs within
90–180 nm range are generated through two major EV biogenesis pathways: EVs (100–
1000 nm) formed through direct plasma membrane budding and exosomes (<200 nm)
originating through the endosomal pathway7-9. In contrast, EV subtype 1 (<90 nm) and EV
subtype 3 (>180 nm) were primarily generated through only one of the two major pathways.
Consequently, the pronounced abundance of EV subtype 2 can be attributed to the
combined output of these two major EV populations. We have further elaborated on the
reasons underlying the abundance variation across the three EV size subtypes in "Steric
hindrance-mediated EV size fractionation".

2. How the PEG layer generates a steric barrier: relate PEG length (14–20 kDa) to the
resulting exclusion distance. Will PEG steric hindrance compromise the recognition ability
of aptamers? Why use aptamers instead of antibodies?
Our response: We gratefully acknowledge the reviewer for their insightful comments
concerning the mechanism of PEG-mediated steric shielding and the rationale for aptamer
selection. As supported by established literature, hydrophilic and flexible PEG chains
grafted onto nanoparticle surfaces extend into the surrounding medium and form hydration
layers through interactions with water molecules, thereby creating a robust steric barrier
that effectively impedes the approach of biomolecules10,11. The extent of this barrier—
commonly referred to as the exclusion distance—is well documented to depend on both
the PEG grafting ratio and molecular weight12,13. Increasing either parameter leads to a
greater exclusion distance and enhanced steric hindrance. Our experimental findings are
fully consistent with this mechanistic (Figure 2 c-f), demonstrating that the binding activity
of surface-conjugated aptamers is precisely regulated by PEG chain length and grafting
ratio. Notably, when PEGs with a molecular weight above 14 kDa were applied at a grafting
ratio of 80% (correspondingly reducing the aptamer grafting ratio to 20%), the resulting
steric exclusion distance was sufficient to effectively reduce aptamer binding affinity by
shielding the aptamer from interacting with CD63 on EV surface. Through systematic
optimization, two distinct MNP formulations were identified that achieved complete steric
shielding of CD63 on EVs larger than 182.9 nm and 93.1 nm in diameter, respectively.
These MNPs were subsequently used to capture EV subpopulations below these size
thresholds, enabling size fractionation of EVs.
Regarding the concern about potential compromise of aptamer function, we would like to
clarify that the steric hindrance introduced by PEG is non-specific and physical in nature.
It does not alter the intrinsic structure of the conjugated aptamers, which retain their
conformation, high-affinity binding sites, and recognition specificity. Instead, the PEG layer
primarily modulates aptamer binding behavior by controlling the rate and probability of
encounters between the target protein and the aptamer. While the PEG chain may reduce
the frequency of collisions between the aptamer and its target protein due to steric shielding,
once contact occurs, the recognition specificity remains unchanged. It is precisely this
mechanism - controlled binding behavior through steric hindrance at the interface - that
enables efficient and selective EV size fractionation. We have clarified this point in the
Discussion section.
We thank the reviewer for raising the point regarding our choice of aptamers over
antibodies. This decision was guided by three main considerations: precise control over
steric hindrance on MNP surfaces, consistent batch-to-batch performance, and the
potential for point-of-care application of the SHEAF platform. Owing to their low molecular
weight and chemically defined synthesis, aptamers enable accurate control of grafting sites
and ratios—factors critical for reliable steric hindrance analysis. In contrast, antibodies
often undergo random conjugation due to their structural complexity14, which increases
inactivation risks and complicates data interpretation. Furthermore, aptamers exhibit
excellent ambient stability and minimal batch variation as they are chemically synthesized,
unlike antibodies, which typically require frozen storage and may exhibit batch-to-batch
variation. These attributes make aptamers not only suitable for controlled experimental
studies but also practical for future translation into robust, point-of-care EV analytical tools.
We have explicitly clarified the rationale for choosing aptamers in the Discussion section.

corroborate the successful size-based fractionation of EVs achieved through our steric
hindrance-mediated method.

Figure 13a). According to NTA and TEM results, the SHEAF platform successfully isolated
EVs with diameters of <90 nm, 90–180 nm, and >180 nm from plasma (new
Supplementary Figure 13b,c). We have incorporated these findings into the revised
manuscript to better address the reviewer’s concern.
5. Clarify why VEGF, TGF-β, PD-L1, CRP, TNF-α, and ICAM-1 were chosen.
Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this important question
regarding our selection of biomarkers. The proteins VEGF, TGF-β, PD-L1, CRP, TNF-α,
and ICAM-1 were carefully chosen based on two main considerations: (1) their well-
established and complementary roles in vascular dysfunction and inflammatory pathways
relevant to stroke pathophysiology; (2) substantiated evidence that these proteins can be
associated on EV membrane. Briefly, VEGF was included for its critical function in
modulating angiogenesis and vascular permeability15; TGF-β for its involvement in immune
regulation, fibrosis, and vascular remodeling16; PD-L1 as a key immune checkpoint
molecule reflecting inflammatory suppression17; CRP as a systemic marker of inflammation
and acute-phase response18; TNF-α for its pro-inflammatory role in BBB disruption and
neuroinflammation19; and ICAM-1 for mediating leukocyte adhesion and endothelial
activation during cerebral ischemia20. Importantly, existing literature confirms that these
proteins have been identified on EV surfaces, supporting their relevance for evaluating EV
biomarker cargo21-23. Together, these markers provide broad coverage of crucial pathways
associated with cerebrovascular and inflammatory injury in stroke.
6. Explain mechanistically why subtype 2 (90–180 nm) is diagnostically superior.
Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for raising this insightful question
regarding the mechanistic basis for the diagnostic superiority of EV subtype 2. We would
like to clarify that this advantage primarily stems from the subtype’s optimal size distribution,
which effectively balances two critical factors: efficient translocation across the BBB and
sufficient membrane surface area for robust biomarker display. Specifically, EVs within the
90–180 nm range (characteristic of subtype 2) demonstrate enhanced efficiency for
crossing the BBB into peripheral circulation1-3. Concurrently, this specific size range
provides an ideal platform for biomarker presentation. EVs smaller than 90 nm often lack
adequate membrane space for displaying a substantial number of specific proteins4,
whereas those larger than 200 nm may frequently incorporate heterogeneous components,
such as apoptotic bodies. Therefore, EV subtype 2 represents a unique population with
both high abundance in blood and ample surface real estate for carrying cell-type-specific,
diagnostically informative markers. Our proteomic analysis confirmed the superior capacity
of EV subtype 2 for carrying a wide range of proteins from various subcellular structures,
including the cytoplasm, cytoskeleton, mitochondria, and nucleus (new Supplementary
Figure 12). In summary, the diagnostic superiority of this EV subpopulation arises from its
balanced capacity for efficient BBB crossing and substantial biomarker-carrying capability.
We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this point and have revised the manuscript
accordingly.
7. Please add more clinical samples and include healthy controls.
Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for highlighting the critical importance of
sample size and the inclusion of healthy controls in our clinical validation. In direct response,
we have significantly expanded our clinical cohort to enhance the statistical robustness of
our findings. Briefly, we collected an additional 20 plasma samples from stroke patients,
including 10 with ischemic stroke (IS) and 10 with intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), along
with 20 plasma samples from healthy donors as a control group.

remain well dispersed under physiological conditions in both culture media and plasma.
This observation aligns with established EV fractionation techniques—such as size-

disaggregation steps and yield well-dispersed, functionally intact EV subpopulations.

In this manuscript entitled “Steric Hindrance-Mediated Extracellular Vesicle Size
Fractionation for Rapid Prehospital Diagnosis of Intracerebral Hemorrhage”, the authors
present a novel SHEAF platform designed to enable rapid EV size-fractionation and protein
profiling. They report that EVs within the 90–180 nm range demonstrate potential as highly
discriminative biomarkers for ICH, with possible applications for rapid and precise stroke
diagnostics in the prehospital setting.
The paper is clearly written, and the investigators provide interesting and timely data.
Nonetheless, several important aspects require clarification and further elaboration. My
detailed comments are outlined below.
1. The introduction is overly superficial. Relevant issues such as cause-specific
management of acute stroke patients in the prehospital setting (e.g., blood pressure control
and the need for ICH patients to be admitted to specialized units) are not addressed. A
more comprehensive rationale for the study design is required, particularly concerning the
potential added value of including EVs. Additionally, the cited literature is somewhat
outdated.
Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for these insightful comments. We have
thoroughly revised the Introduction to address these concerns. Briefly, we have expanded
the explanation of cause‑specific prehospital management in acute stroke, now clearly
differentiating the early protocols for ICH and IS. These include the emphasis on rapid
blood‑pressure control and direct triage to specialized neurocritical care units for ICH
patients, as opposed to time‑sensitive reperfusion therapies for IS patients. This
enhancement strengthens the clinical rationale for rapid prehospital differentiation of stroke
subtypes, a central theme of our study.
In response to the reviewer’s comment, we have refined the rationale to highlight the added
value of EV in Introduction section. The SHEAF platform addresses the critical unmet
need for prehospital diagnosis when timely neuroimaging is unavailable. EVs serve as
ideal circulating biomarkers in this context because they cross the BBB and transport brain-
specific biomarkers (e.g., VEGF, TNF-α) into circulation. Furthermore, EVs can protect
encapsulated biomarkers from degradation, thereby offering enhanced specificity and
stability compared to free biomarkers. However, EV heterogeneity—especially
polydisperse sizes—reduces diagnostic accuracy. To overcome this, our SHEAF platform
employs steric hindrance-mediated size fractionation to selectively isolate EV subtypes
(e.g., 90–180 nm) that optimally balance barrier penetration and biomarker load. This
enriches disease-specific signals while reducing background noise. By integrating this
unique biological property of EVs with a sub-45-min workflow, the SHEAF platform enables
accurate ICH/IS discrimination without imaging, providing a rapid biomarker-based tool to
improve prehospital stroke triage.
Finally, we have updated the cited literature with references from the last five years. At the
same time, references on aptamer development (reporting Kd values) and curvature-
dependent binding of phospholipids at the EV surface have been retained as originally
cited.
2. The methodological section is insufficiently detailed. Critical clinical information is
missing, such as patient recruitment details (e.g., location, timeframe), laboratory where
analyses were performed, and whether assays were conducted in a blinded manner. The
timing of sample collection—fundamental to the claimed prehospital application—is not
reported. The statistical methods are inadequately described, with no mention of sample
size calculation, limited descriptive statistics, and no adjustment for multiple comparisons.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out the missing of clinical information.
That critical information has been provided in the revised manuscript. Specifically, clinical
samples of stroke patients were collected at the Department of emergency of The Affiliated
Hospital of Guizhou Medical University, while clinical samples of healthy controls were
collected at the Department of Cardiovascular Medicine. The initial cohort of samples was
collected from January to September 2024, while the additional samples incorporated
during the revision phase were obtained between August and October 2025. Clinical
diagnoses were performed by medical staff from the Department of Emergency Medicine
and the Department of Cardiovascular Medicine. Subsequent analyses based on SHEAF
platform were conducted by researchers from the School of Pharmacy at Guizhou Medical
University and School of Mechanical Engineering at Northwestern Polytechnical University.
All sample-related assays were performed in a blinded manner. For stroke patients, blood
was collected prior to any treatment intervention. Diagnosis of either ICH or IS was
confirmed within one hour after blood sampling. For healthy donors, blood samples were
obtained from individuals with no history of stroke or myocardial infarction. For clarification,
we have revised the “Clinical samples” section and added a baseline characteristics table
as new Supplementary Table 2.
We are grateful to the reviewer for the valuable suggestion to enhance the statistical rigor
of our study. Accordingly, we have revised the Statistics section to include a sample size
calculation for the clinical analyses and have incorporated false discovery rate adjustments
for multiple comparisons. The detailed results of these analyses are now provided in new

with a combined AUC value of 0.958 (revised Figure 5c and new Supplementary Figure

Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that
the current requirement for plasma processing, together with an ~45-min workflow, poses
practical challenges for immediate deployment and routine operation in an ambulance
setting. Nevertheless, SHEAF was conceived as a compact platform that operates without
large, fixed instruments, which provides a realistic pathway toward future prehospital use
under resource- and space-constrained conditions. In practice, plasma preparation could
be enabled by pairing SHEAF with a portable centrifuge, allowing sample processing
directly after collection within the ambulance compartment. Importantly, initiating the assay
during patient transport shifts testing earlier in the care pathway; thus, even with the current
~45-min workflow, results could be available either en route or shortly after hospital arrival,
thereby shortening the time to clinical decision-making. We emphasize, however, that
further workflow optimization (e.g., reducing processing time and simplifying sample
handling) and validation in real-world prehospital settings will be required before routine
clinical implementation. We have clarified these aspects in the revised Discussion.
5. The statement that the platform outperforms “conventional approaches” is vague, as no
clear comparator methods are identified.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We fully acknowledge
that computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) represent the
current gold standard for stroke diagnosis, delivering exceptional diagnostic accuracy and
detailed anatomical information essential for guiding treatment decisions. The key
strengths of our platform lie in its markedly shorter end-to-end time compared to the
logistical delays of CT/MRI acquisition, as well as its potential in resource-limited settings
that lack immediate access to advanced neuroimaging (new Supplementary Table 4). To
clarify this distinction, we have revised the Discussion to explicitly state that the SHEAF
platform is intended as a rapid supplementary tool—not a replacement—for established
imaging modalities, facilitating earlier triage and intervention during the prehospital phase
of stroke care.

We also acknowledge the concern about the reliability of ROC analyses given the initial
sample size. In our study, we used the leave-one-out method—a technique appropriate for
small clinical datasets—to generate the ROC curves. Furthermore, during the revision
period, we collected additional patient samples to enhance the statistical robustness of our
conclusions.
The reviewer noted that most individual proteins showed limited discriminatory power (AUC
0.6–0.7), which we agree is consistent with the multifactorial nature of stroke. It is widely
recognized that a single biomarker may be insufficient to capture the complexity of such
diseases, whereas a combination of biomarkers can reflect complementary pathways38,
thereby improving overall classification performance—as demonstrated by the higher AUC
achieved by the six-protein panel.
In accordance with the reviewer's suggestion, we have removed the phrase "near-ideal
classification accuracy" to ensure a more precise description of the diagnostic performance.
The previously missing metrics—including cut-off values, sensitivity, and specificity—have

sensitivity and specificity were 0.88 and 0.92, respectively, in differentiating ICH from IS,
and 0.84 and 0.95, respectively, in distinguishing stroke from healthy controls. We believe
these revisions have significantly enhanced the statistical rigor and clarity of the manuscript.

underlying the superior performance of subtype 2 EVs. Moreover, there is no consideration
of the optimal diagnostic time window for the proposed approach.
Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for their insightful comment regarding the
biological rationale for the superior performance of subtype 2 EVs. The enhanced
diagnostic capability of this subset stems from its optimal size, which uniquely balances
efficient translocation across BBB with substantial biomarker-carrying capacity. Specifically,
EVs within the 90–180 nm range are sufficiently small to traverse the BBB effectively1-3,
facilitating their release into circulation after stroke, while also providing greater membrane
surface area for robust presentation of cell-type-specific markers compared to smaller EVs
(<90 nm)4. Moreover, EVs larger than 180 nm often represent apoptotic bodies and exhibit
greater heterogeneity. In support of this, our proteomic analysis revealed that subtype 2
contains a significantly higher number of proteins of subcellular origin compared to both
subtype 1 (<90 nm) and subtype 3 (>180 nm) (new Supplementary Figure 12).
Regarding the optimal diagnostic time window, we agree on its critical importance for
clinical translation. In alignment with stroke management guidelines that emphasize
intervention as early as possible to prevent irreversible brain injury, we propose that blood
sampling for the SHEAF platform should be performed immediately upon patient
presentation. Notably, unlike conventional diagnostic approaches that can only be
conducted after hospital arrival, our method holds potential for prehospital use—such as
during ambulance transport—enabling significantly earlier diagnosis. This shift forward in
the diagnostic timeline allows crucial treatment decisions (e.g., thrombolysis or surgery) to
be made sooner upon arrival, thereby preserving the “time is brain” principle and improving
patient outcomes. We have revised the Discussion to highlight this advantage of early,
time-sensitive application of our approach.

Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for highlighting these important limitations
regarding our initial cohort. In direct response to the comments, we have expanded the
clinical cohort to include additional samples—specifically, 10 ICH, 10 IS, and 20 healthy
donors as a control group—which has strengthened the statistical reliability of our findings.
To improve transparency and allow for a better assessment of potential confounders, we
have also included a new patient information table (new Supplementary Table 2)
summarizing age, sex, and comorbidities. We clarify that for all stroke patients, blood was
collected prior to any treatment intervention, and the diagnosis of either ICH or IS was
confirmed within one hour after blood sampling.
While the expanded sample size represents a meaningful improvement, we acknowledge
that further scaling through larger, multicenter studies will be important to support the
broader applicability of our findings. As such, we have explicitly discussed the current
cohort size in the Discussion section, framing it as a focused foundation for future
validation. We also emphasize that this work provides a robust methodological platform
and preliminary clinical evidence, paving the way for subsequent multi-institutional
collaborations aimed at prehospital translation.
